第二層調査




R01だけを根拠にしてはいけない。




2026年現在の外部研究・標準・実装から、以下を独立に調査する。




A. ApprovalとAuthorization




Human approvalは、




「記録された人間のクリック」




なのか、




「execution authority」




なのか。




両者を区別する現在の研究・実装が存在するか確認する。




B. Pre-authorization

存在する場合、




scope

context

identity

policy version

validity

expiry

revocation




の束縛がどこまで要求されているか確認する。




C. Runtime再検証




特に重要。




approval後からexecutionまでの間に、




scope change

context change

policy change

identity change

boundary drift

stale approval

retry

replay

alternate execution path

side channel




が発生した場合、execution直前にauthorizationを再評価する設計が現在どの程度一般化しているか確認する。




D. Human Gate




Human-in-the-loopとHuman Authorityを区別する資料を探す。




「humanが介在した」という事実だけではauthorityの成立を証明できない、という考え方が一次資料または信頼できる研究で確認できるか調査する。




E. Decision Window




R01の最も重要な論点。




「decision windowが短い／実質的にdeliberationできない」という状況を、




architecture

interface

workflow

doctrine

policy

organizational process




が生成している可能性について、現在の研究・ガバナンス論が何を述べているか調査する。

approval時点では検証されるが、execution時点に独立したre-verificationおよびHuman Stop Pointが存在しない




との対応を検証する。

各主張を次の4分類に分ける。




CONFIRMED




一次資料または複数の独立した信頼できる資料によって支持される。




SUPPORTED




有力な資料によって支持されるが、一次Evidenceとしては不十分。

第五層




最後に、MoCKAへの扱いを判定する。




Adopt

Reject / Do Not Promote

最重要監査質問




今回の調査では、単に




「R01は正しいか」




を問わない。




最終的に以下を回答する。




Approval recordは、execution時点におけるHuman Authorityの成立を証明できるか。




そして、




Pre-authorizationが存在する場合、それだけでruntime authorizationを代替できるか。




さらに、




「Humanが判断できなかった」というdecision window自体が、architecture・interface・process・doctrineによって生成された場合、そのwindowをauthorityの根拠として扱ってよいのか。

\begin{abstract}

Paper 3.5$\zeta$ presents an evidence-bound framework for empirically
qualifying the boundary between institutional human authority and
consequential runtime execution. It is positioned between Paper
3.5$\beta$, which specifies institutional and authorization boundaries,
and Paper 4, which addresses origin propagation and
transformation-aware provenance.

The central research question is:

\begin{quote}
Can institutional authorization actually constrain consequential execution
at runtime?
\end{quote}

The study distinguishes four properties of authorization:
Authorization Existence, Authorization Validity, Authorization Reachability,
and Authorization Enforcement. These properties are ordered as increasing
assurance requirements rather than logical implications:

\[
A_E \prec A_V \prec A_R \prec A_F.
\]

The R04 investigation produced three Human Gate findings, HG-01--03,
and a separate architectural reachability claim, AR-01. Their normative
reconstruction statuses are maintained exclusively in Appendix B and
remain subject to authoritative source binding at the present manuscript
stage.

The paper therefore separates structural meaning, narrative
reconstruction, and empirical verification:

\[
\text{Structural Meaning}
\neq
\text{Narrative Reconstruction}
\neq
\text{Verified Empirical Finding}.
\]

The paper further defines a target runtime invariant for consequential
actions:

\[
\forall a \in \mathbb{A}_{\mathrm{consequential}},
\quad
\neg\operatorname{VerifiedAuthorization}(a,c,t)
\Rightarrow
\neg\operatorname{Execute}(a,c,t).
\]

This is presented as a target invariant and architectural requirement,
not as a claim that the historical system already satisfied it.

The study also preserves incomplete provenance reconstruction as an
Evidence Gap rather than treating non-reconstruction as evidence of
nonexistence. Complete provenance traceability is therefore handed forward
to Paper 4 without silently resolving unresolved origin links.

The resulting architectural boundary is:

\[
\text{Human Authority}
\rightarrow
\text{Bound Authorization}
\rightarrow
\text{Reachable Verification}
\rightarrow
\text{Enforcement}
\rightarrow
\text{Consequential Execution}.
\]

\end{abstract}

% ============================================================
\section{Introduction and Research Position}
\label{sec:introduction}
% ============================================================

Paper 3.5$\zeta$ addresses a specific boundary in the development of the
Evidence-Bound Governance Architecture (EBGA): the transition from
institutional authority to technically constrained execution.

Earlier work established that AI governance cannot be reduced to the
presence of a human decision, a policy statement, or an evidence record.
A governance system must preserve uncertainty, distinguish authorization
from capability, and prevent unsupported states from silently becoming
authoritative states.

Paper 3.5$\beta$ therefore specified an institutional boundary in which
Human Gate decisions, evidence, authorization, and execution were
explicitly separated.

The empirical question left open by that specification is more demanding:

\begin{quote}
Does the institutional authorization boundary actually reach the runtime
execution boundary?
\end{quote}

This paper calls that question \emph{boundary qualification}.

The purpose of Paper 3.5$\zeta$ is not to establish a complete theory of
provenance, nor to solve origin propagation. Its purpose is to determine,
within a defined evidence scope and examined execution path, whether the
institutional authorization boundary is structurally connected to
consequential execution.

The central conceptual transition is therefore:

\[
\text{Uncertainty Management}
\neq
\text{Execution Control}.
\]

A system may preserve UNKNOWN states correctly while still permitting
an action to cross an execution boundary without a verified authorization.
Conversely, the existence of a Human Gate does not establish that the
runtime respects its outcome.

The principal contribution of this paper is consequently a separation
between:

\[
\text{Authorization Existence},
\quad
\text{Authorization Validity},
\quad
\text{Authorization Reachability},
\quad
\text{Authorization Enforcement}.
\]

% ============================================================
\section{Research Genealogy and Boundary}
\label{sec:genealogy}
% ============================================================

The research sequence is:

\[
\text{Paper 1}
\rightarrow
\text{Paper 2}
\rightarrow
\text{Paper 3}
\rightarrow
\text{Paper 3.5$\alpha$}
\rightarrow
\text{Paper 3.5$\beta$}
\rightarrow
\text{Paper 3.5$\zeta$}
\rightarrow
\text{Paper 4}.
\]

Paper 3 established the semantic distinction between UNKNOWN, REM,
confirmed states, and unresolved states. It also established that
compression is not resolution and that absence of evidence must not be
converted into a false certainty.

Paper 3.5$\alpha$ froze the theoretical and empirical verification
boundary.

Paper 3.5$\beta$ then specified institutional boundaries, including the
distinction:

\[
\text{Specification}
\neq
\text{Verification}
\neq
\text{Authorization}
\neq
\text{Deployment}
\neq
\text{Evidence}.
\]

Paper 3.5$\zeta$ empirically qualifies whether those institutional
boundaries are connected to runtime execution.

Paper 4 is reserved for origin propagation, composition, transformation,
and transformation-aware provenance.

Thus:

\[
\boxed{
\text{Paper 3.5$\zeta$ is not Paper 4.}
}
\]

The unresolved provenance boundary is intentionally preserved for that
later work.

% ============================================================
\section{Inherited Semantic and Institutional Boundaries}
\label{sec:inherited-boundaries}
% ============================================================

Paper 3.5$\zeta$ inherits several non-negotiable semantic rules.

\subsection{UNKNOWN is not FALSE}
\label{sec:unknown-not-false}

The absence of sufficient evidence does not establish the falsity of a
proposition:

\[
\text{No Evidence}
\not\Rightarrow
\text{False}.
\]

Likewise:

\[
\text{Not Found}
\not\Rightarrow
\text{Does Not Exist}.
\]

\subsection{Evidence is not Authorization}
\label{sec:evidence-not-authorization}

The existence of an evidence record does not itself create authority:

\[
\text{Evidence}
\not\Rightarrow
\text{Authorization}.
\]

Similarly:

\[
\text{No Source} + \text{No Human Decision}
\Rightarrow
\text{No New Authority}.
\]

\subsection{Authorization is not Execution}
\label{sec:authorization-not-execution}

An authorization record does not itself demonstrate that execution is
constrained by that authorization:

\[
\text{Authorization}
\not\Rightarrow
\text{Execution Control}.
\]

Conversely, the fact that execution occurred does not prove that valid
authorization existed beforehand.

\subsection{Narrative coherence is not empirical verification}
\label{sec:narrative-not-verification}

A reconstruction can be internally coherent while remaining empirically
unverified:

\[
\text{Narrative Reconstruction}
\not\Rightarrow
\text{Verified}.
\]

This principle is applied to the paper's own claims.

% ============================================================
\section{Method and Evidence Scope}
\label{sec:method}
% ============================================================

\subsection{Evidence Scope}
\label{sec:evidence-scope}

The empirical claims in this paper are limited to the defined R04
investigation scope and the execution path examined during that
investigation.

The evidence scope includes, where applicable:

\begin{itemize}
    \item R04 Phase A records;
    \item R04 Phase B runtime and boundary observations;
    \item R04 Phase C provenance investigation and closeout records;
    \item R04 remediation records;
    \item execution traces and authorization-state observations;
    \item Human Gate decision records;
    \item relevant primary logs, configuration records, and contemporaneous
          execution evidence;
    \item authoritative source identifiers associated with the above.
\end{itemize}

Exact evidence identifiers are intentionally not inferred from narrative
summaries. They must be inserted from the authoritative R04 records.

\subsection{Three methodological layers}
\label{sec:methodological-layers}

The empirical methodology separates three layers.

\paragraph{Evidence Scope.}
What records and execution paths are admissible?

\paragraph{Reconstruction Rule.}
What relationship may be reconstructed from those records?

\paragraph{Claim Qualification.}
What status is justified after reconstruction?

Thus:

\[
\text{Source}
\rightarrow
\text{Scope}
\rightarrow
\text{Reconstruction Rule}
\rightarrow
\text{Claim Status}.
\]

\subsection{Evidence-state vocabulary}
\label{sec:evidence-vocabulary}

The following terms are used strictly.

\begin{description}[leftmargin=38mm]

    \item[\Observed]
    An event or attribute directly recorded by an authoritative primary
    source.

    \item[\Reconstructed]
    A local relationship reconstructed from observed records according to
    an explicit reconstruction rule.

    \item[\Verified Within Scope]
    A claim for which the authoritative source identifier, scope,
    reconstruction rule, contextual correspondence, and applicable
    qualification conditions are satisfied.

    \item[\NotEstablished]
    A claim that cannot be established after a completed reconstruction
    procedure under a defined evidence scope and completion criterion.

    \item[\PendingSourceBinding]
    A structurally defined claim for which the required authoritative
    evidence identifier has not yet been bound to the claim record.

    \item[\PartiallyEstablished]
    A claim for which some required relations are established but the
    complete qualification criterion is not satisfied.

    \item[\Required]
    A future architectural or governance requirement rather than a
    historical empirical observation.

    \item[\TargetInvariant]
    A formal property that a compliant implementation is required to
    satisfy.

\end{description}

The distinction

\[
\text{\PendingSourceBinding}
\neq
\text{\NotEstablished}
\]

is fundamental.

The former concerns incomplete evidence binding.

The latter concerns a completed reconstruction procedure whose required
claim could not be established within the defined scope.

% ============================================================
\section{R04 Evidence Mapping}
\label{sec:r04-mapping}
% ============================================================

The R04 investigation is divided into three empirical phases.

\begin{table}[ht]
\centering
\caption{R04-to-Paper 3.5$\zeta$ Evidence Mapping}
\begin{tabular}{p{22mm}p{55mm}p{65mm}}
\toprule
\textbf{R04 Phase} &
\textbf{Investigation Target} &
\textbf{Paper 3.5$\zeta$ Use} \\
\midrule
Phase A &
Human Gate premise, required decision boundary, and institutional
authorization conditions &
Human Gate qualification and authorization existence/validity analysis
\\
Phase B &
Runtime authorization and execution-boundary observations &
Authorization reachability and enforcement analysis
\\
Phase C &
Provenance reconstruction and closure &
Evidence Gap qualification and Paper 4 handoff
\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

The exact source identifiers for each phase shall be inserted from the
authoritative R04 records and shall not be inferred from secondary
summaries.

The evidence mapping is subject to the Source Binding Rule defined in
Appendix~\ref{sec:appendix-c}.

% ============================================================
\section{Human Gate Findings}
\label{sec:human-gate-findings}
% ============================================================

The Human Gate findings are identified as HG-01, HG-02, and HG-03.
They are distinct from AR-01, which is an architectural Authorization
Reachability claim concerning the relationship between institutional
authorization and the runtime execution path.

The normative reconstruction status of the Human Gate claims is maintained
in Appendix~\ref{sec:appendix-b}.

\subsection{HG-01: Human Gate decision requirement}
\label{sec:hg01}

The R04 investigation identified a Human Gate decision as a required
governance checkpoint for the relevant phase.

At the structural level:

\[
\text{Required Human Decision}
\rightarrow
\text{Authorization Boundary}.
\]

However, the existence of such a requirement does not by itself establish
that the corresponding decision was converted into a runtime-enforceable
authorization.

The normative status of HG-01 is recorded in Appendix~\ref{sec:appendix-b},
Claim C-01.

\subsection{HG-02: Human Gate checkpoint was not technically blocking}
\label{sec:hg02}

The examined path indicates that the relevant checkpoint did not constitute
a technically blocking execution boundary.

The critical distinction is:

\[
\text{Human Gate Exists}
\not\Rightarrow
\text{Execution is Blocked}.
\]

A checkpoint may exist institutionally while the runtime path remains
capable of proceeding.

The normative status of HG-02 is recorded in Appendix~\ref{sec:appendix-b},
Claim C-02.

\subsection{HG-03: Pre-decision execution}
\label{sec:hg03}

The investigation reconstructed a case characterized structurally as
execution occurring before the required authorization decision had been
established.

The critical temporal relation is:

\[
t_{\mathrm{execution}}
<
t_{\mathrm{verified\ authorization}}.
\]

However, this relation can only be treated as a verified empirical
qualification when the following conditions are satisfied:

\begin{enumerate}
    \item the same action is identified on both sides;
    \item authorization and execution scopes are comparable;
    \item the execution context is identifiable;
    \item authorization state is established as \emph{verified}, not merely
          present;
    \item timestamps have known provenance, precision, ordering, and
          timezone semantics;
    \item the execution event is established as consequential under
          Claim C-06 and
          Sec.~\ref{sec:consequential-actions};
    \item the evidence is connected to authoritative primary records;
    \item no disqualifying contradiction remains unresolved.
\end{enumerate}

Thus C-03 is dependent on the consequential-action qualification represented
by C-06. The existence of a pre-decision execution event alone does not
automatically establish a pre-decision \emph{consequential} execution.

The normative status of HG-03 is recorded in Appendix~\ref{sec:appendix-b},
Claim C-03.

% ============================================================
\section{Authorization Reachability Claim}
\label{sec:authorization-reachability-claim}
% ============================================================

AR-01 is deliberately separated from the Human Gate findings.

It is an architectural reconstruction claim concerning whether an
applicable authorization can actually reach and be verified by the
runtime execution boundary.

The central question is:

\[
\text{Can the Execution Boundary Reach and Verify the Applicable Authorization?}
\]

The bounded candidate qualification is:

\[
A_R
\text{ was not established from the available evidence for the examined
path under the defined reconstruction criterion}.
\]

This statement does not imply that authorization reachability is absent
from the system as a whole, nor that no other execution path could satisfy
the reachability condition.

HG-02 and HG-03 provide related observations for this architectural
question, but they do not automatically verify AR-01.

The normative status of AR-01 is maintained through Claim C-04 in
Appendix~\ref{sec:appendix-b}.

% ============================================================
\section{Authorization as a Multi-Property Boundary}
\label{sec:authorization-properties}
% ============================================================

Authorization is not treated as a binary object.

Four distinct assurance properties are defined:

\[
A_E = \text{Authorization Existence},
\]

\[
A_V = \text{Authorization Validity},
\]

\[
A_R = \text{Authorization Reachability},
\]

\[
A_F = \text{Authorization Enforcement}.
\]

They are ordered as:

\[
\boxed{
A_E \prec A_V \prec A_R \prec A_F
}
\]

where $\prec$ denotes increasing assurance requirements and dependency
strength. It does \emph{not} denote logical implication.

In particular:

\[
A_E \not\Rightarrow A_V,
\]

\[
A_E \land A_V \not\Rightarrow A_R,
\]

and

\[
A_R \not\Rightarrow A_F.
\]

The four properties should therefore never be collapsed into a single
``authorized'' boolean without preserving the underlying distinctions.

% ============================================================
\section{Authorization Existence}
\label{sec:authorization-existence}
% ============================================================

Authorization Existence concerns whether a formally recognizable
authorization state or record exists.

To avoid notation collision with the action universe, the authorization
artifact is represented as $\mathsf{Auth}$:

\[
\mathsf{Auth}
=
(
id,
issuer,
subject,
action,
scope,
evidenceRef,
context,
issuedAt,
expiresAt,
revocationState,
integrity
).
\]

Existence alone does not establish that the authorization is valid,
applicable, current, or connected to execution.

% ============================================================
\section{Authorization Validity}
\label{sec:authorization-validity}
% ============================================================

Authorization Validity concerns whether an authorization is valid for the
relevant action, scope, evidence, context, and time.

Validity therefore requires more than the existence of a historical record.

A valid authorization should at minimum establish:

\begin{itemize}
    \item decision authority;
    \item authorized action;
    \item authorized scope;
    \item evidence basis;
    \item applicable context;
    \item validity interval;
    \item current state;
    \item integrity of the authorization record.
\end{itemize}

An authorization that has been superseded, revoked, expired, or rendered
inapplicable does not satisfy the validity requirement.

A sealed Human Gate decision may be represented separately as:

\[
\mathsf{Dec}
=
(
decisionId,
decider,
decision,
scope,
evidenceRef,
issuedAt,
integrity
).
\]

The separation between $\mathsf{Dec}$ and $\mathsf{Auth}$ preserves the
distinction between a human decision and the machine-consumable
authorization derived from that decision.

% ============================================================
\section{Authorization Reachability}
\label{sec:authorization-reachability}
% ============================================================

Authorization Reachability concerns whether the runtime execution
boundary can obtain and verify the authorization that governs the
action being executed.

This is a structural property.

A valid authorization may exist in an institutional record while being
unreachable from the execution path.

Therefore:

\[
A_V \not\Rightarrow A_R.
\]

A system that stores authorization correctly but cannot reliably bind the
execution event to that authorization has not established runtime
authorization reachability.

This is the architectural property represented by AR-01.

% ============================================================
\section{Authorization Enforcement}
\label{sec:authorization-enforcement}
% ============================================================

Authorization Enforcement is stronger than reachability.

A runtime may successfully retrieve an authorization and verify it while
still permitting execution through an alternative or bypass path.

Therefore:

\[
A_R \not\Rightarrow A_F.
\]

Authorization Enforcement requires a structural dependency between
authorization verification and consequential execution.

The required property is not merely:

\[
\text{Authorization can be checked}.
\]

It is:

\[
\text{Execution cannot successfully cross the consequential boundary
without successful authorization verification}.
\]

A runtime verification function can therefore be represented as:

\[
\operatorname{Verify}(\mathsf{Auth},a,c,t).
\]

Verification is meaningful only when the authorization artifact,
action, scope, context, and time are correspondingly bound.

% ============================================================
\section{Consequential Actions}
\label{sec:consequential-actions}
% ============================================================

The enforcement invariant is intentionally restricted to consequential
actions.

Let the complete action space be:

\[
\mathbb{A}
=
\mathbb{A}_{\mathrm{nonconsequential}}
\cup
\mathbb{A}_{\mathrm{consequential}}.
\]

Non-consequential actions may include internal reasoning, drafting,
simulation, analysis, or preparation that does not itself produce a
consequential external effect.

Consequential actions include, depending on system context:

\begin{itemize}
    \item modification of an external system;
    \item transmission of information to an external recipient;
    \item command of a physical or operational process;
    \item irreversible or institutionally consequential state updates;
    \item financial or contractual commitment;
    \item privilege or authorization assignment;
    \item state transitions that enable subsequent consequential actions.
\end{itemize}

The examined execution discussed in HG-03 is classified as a consequential
action under this definition only when the authoritative evidence binding
establishes that it crossed one of these consequential boundaries.

This classification is itself subject to source binding and is not
silently assumed merely because an execution event occurred.

The normative status of this classification is maintained through Claim
C-06 in Appendix~\ref{sec:appendix-b}.

% ============================================================
\section{Scope Preservation}
\label{sec:scope-preservation}
% ============================================================

Authorization scope must not expand merely because execution occurs.

The required relationship is:

\[
\operatorname{Scope}(\operatorname{Execution})
\subseteq
\operatorname{Scope}(\operatorname{Authorization}).
\]

Any execution whose effective scope exceeds the authorization scope is
therefore outside the authorized boundary.

This principle applies independently of whether the underlying
authorization record exists.

% ============================================================
\section{Sealed Authorization}
\label{sec:sealed-authorization}
% ============================================================

A Human Gate decision becomes operationally meaningful only when it is
converted into a sealed authorization state that can be independently
referenced by the execution boundary.

A sealed authorization should include at minimum:

\begin{itemize}
    \item decision-maker identity;
    \item decision identifier;
    \item decision version;
    \item authorized action;
    \item authorized scope;
    \item evidence reference;
    \item applicable context;
    \item timestamp;
    \item integrity protection;
    \item revocation or supersession state;
    \item machine-readable execution reference.
\end{itemize}

Thus:

\[
\text{Human Gate Decision}
\rightarrow
\text{SEALED}
\rightarrow
\text{Verified Authorization}.
\]

A narrative statement that a human ``approved'' an action is insufficient
unless the authorization can be bound to the execution-relevant state.

% ============================================================
\section{In-Flight Reverification}
\label{sec:in-flight-reverification}
% ============================================================

Authorization should be verified immediately before the consequential
side effect rather than only at an earlier planning checkpoint.

A runtime architecture should therefore support:

\[
\text{Authorization Verification}
\rightarrow
\text{Immediate Execution Boundary Check}
\rightarrow
\text{Consequential Execution}.
\]

If any material execution condition changes between approval and execution,
the authorization must be re-evaluated.

Material changes include, at minimum:

\begin{itemize}
    \item action identity;
    \item execution scope;
    \item execution context;
    \item relevant evidence;
    \item authorization state;
    \item execution-relevant code or system snapshot.
\end{itemize}

An authorization that is no longer applicable must not be treated as
evergreen permission.

% ============================================================
\section{Block versus Execution Failure}
\label{sec:block-versus-failure}
% ============================================================

The concepts of ``DENY'' and ``not executed'' are not treated as
identical.

If authorization is absent or invalid, the runtime should enter a
blocking state:

\[
\neg\operatorname{VerifiedAuthorization}(a,c,t)
\Rightarrow
\operatorname{Block}(a,c,t).
\]

The blocking mechanism may take several forms:

\[
\operatorname{Block}
\in
\{
\operatorname{DENY},
\operatorname{WAIT},
\operatorname{CANCEL},
\operatorname{ESCALATE},
\operatorname{SAFE\_FALLBACK}
\}.
\]

Here, $\operatorname{Block}$ is a control state or control action and is
not synonymous with $\operatorname{DENY}$.

The stronger execution property is then:

\[
\operatorname{Block}(a,c,t)
\Rightarrow
\neg\operatorname{Execute}(a,c,t).
\]

This separation permits safety-oriented fallback behavior without
conflating all forms of non-execution with a conventional ``DENY'' state.

Any emergency or break-glass mechanism must be governed by a separately
defined policy rather than silently bypassing the Human Gate boundary.

\label{sec:target-runtime-invariant}
% ============================================================

\paragraph{\TargetInvariant.}

For every consequential action:

\forall a \in \mathbb{A}_{\mathrm{consequential}},
\quad

\neg\operatorname{Execute}(a,c,t)

for:

\[

examined system already satisfied it.

\paragraph{\Required.}

between authorization verification and the consequential execution path.

Operationally, the target invariant may be decomposed as:

\[

\Rightarrow
\operatorname{Block}(a,c,t)
\]

and:

\[

\Rightarrow

\]

% ============================================================
\section{Two Chains: Authority and Execution}
\label{sec:two-chains}
% ============================================================

Two distinct chains must remain visible.

The institutional authority chain is:

\[
\text{Human Decision}
\rightarrow
\text{Institutional Authorization}
\rightarrow
\text{Sealed Authorization}.
\]

The runtime execution chain is:

\[
\text{Execution Request}
\rightarrow
\text{Authorization Resolution}
\rightarrow
\text{Verification}
\rightarrow
\text{Execution Boundary}
\rightarrow
\text{Consequential Execution}.
\]

Governance exists only when the two chains are structurally connected.

The required architecture is therefore:

\[
\boxed{
\text{Institutional Authority}
\xrightarrow{\text{bound authorization + runtime verification}}
\text{Runtime Enforcement}
}
\]

rather than merely:

\[
\text{Institutional Authority}
\rightarrow
\text{Documentation}.
\]

An effective governance condition can be represented as:

\[
\boxed{
\operatorname{EffectiveGovernance}(a,c,t)
=
\operatorname{ValidInstitutionalAuthority}(a,c,t)
\land
\operatorname{EnforcedRuntimeConstraint}(a,c,t)
}
\]

for consequential actions.

\section{Institutional Control Surface}
\label{sec:institutional-control-surface}
% ============================================================

The institutional control surface can be represented as:

\[
\text{Governance Defines}
\rightarrow
\text{Enforcement Prevents}
\rightarrow
\text{Evidence Proves}.
\]

These functions are distinct.

Detection does not equal prevention:

\[
\text{Detection}
\neq
\text{Prevention}.
\]

Evidence of an unauthorized execution after the fact does not establish
that the governance mechanism prevented it.

Likewise:

\[
\text{Evidence of Violation}
\neq
\text{Enforcement Against Violation}.
\]

This distinction is central to the transition from Paper 3.5$\beta$ to
Paper 3.5$\zeta$.

\section{Assurance Ordering and Logical Non-Implication}
\label{sec:assurance-ordering}
% ============================================================

The four authorization properties form an assurance ladder:

\[
\boxed{
A_E \prec A_V \prec A_R \prec A_F
}
\]

where the relation $\prec$ represents increasing assurance requirements
and dependency strength.

It must not be interpreted as logical implication.

In particular:

\[
A_E \not\Rightarrow A_V,
\]

\[
A_E \land A_V \not\Rightarrow A_R,
\]

\[
A_R \not\Rightarrow A_F.
\]

This distinction prevents an authorization artifact from being treated as
evidence that runtime enforcement exists.

The ladder can therefore be interpreted as:

\[
\begin{array}{ll}
A_E &: \text{Does an authorization object exist?}\\
A_V &: \text{Is that authorization valid for the relevant action?}\\
A_R &: \text{Can the execution boundary reach and verify it?}\\
A_F &: \text{Does execution structurally depend on successful verification?}
\end{array}
\]

The highest assurance point addressed by Paper 3.5$\zeta$ is therefore
Authorization Enforcement, not merely Authorization Existence.

\section{Discussion}
\label{sec:discussion}
% ============================================================

Within the defined conceptual model and the examined R04 reconstruction
target, the study identifies why the existence of a Human Gate, an
approval record, or an authorization state is insufficient by itself to
establish runtime governance.

The corresponding empirical claims remain subject to the authoritative
source-binding process defined in Appendix~\ref{sec:appendix-c}.

The progression is:

\[
\text{Human Authority}
\rightarrow
\text{Bound Authorization}
\rightarrow
\text{Reachable Verification}
\rightarrow
\text{Enforcement}
\rightarrow
\text{Consequential Execution}.
\]

The key architectural distinction is therefore:

\[
\text{Approval}
\neq
\text{Authorization}
\neq
\text{Execution}.
\]

A system may have all three concepts in documentation while lacking the
structural dependency necessary for enforcement.

The important engineering implication is not that AI must be prevented
from performing autonomous analysis.

Rather:

\[
\text{AI Autonomy}
\]

may remain available for:

\begin{itemize}
    \item analysis;
    \item reasoning;
    \item simulation;
    \item proposal generation;
    \item drafting;
    \item preparation.
\end{itemize}

The critical boundary is the transition:

\[
\text{Proposal}
\rightarrow
\text{Authorized Action}
\rightarrow
\text{Consequential State Transition}.
\]

This transition must be controlled.

Therefore:

\[
\text{Default Deny}
\neq
\text{Universal Inaction}.
\]

Default deny applies to consequential execution in the absence of verified
authorization.

\section{Architectural Implications}
\label{sec:architectural-implications}
% ============================================================

The empirical qualification framework produces three primary
architectural requirements.

\subsection{Default-Deny at the consequential boundary}
\label{sec:default-deny}

The runtime must not permit a consequential action to proceed when
verified authorization is absent.

\[
\neg\operatorname{VerifiedAuthorization}
\Rightarrow
\operatorname{Block}.
\]

\subsection{Capability-based authorization}
\label{sec:capability-authorization}

Human authority should be represented as a bounded authorization
capability rather than as an unstructured approval statement.

The authorization artifact should encode:

\[
\mathsf{Auth}
=
(
id,
issuer,
subject,
action,
scope,
evidenceRef,
context,
issuedAt,
expiresAt,
revocationState,
integrity
).
\]

\subsection{In-flight reverification}
\label{sec:architectural-reverification}

The runtime should re-check authorization immediately before the
consequential side effect.

This prevents stale authorization from becoming implicit authority.

\label{sec:paper4-boundary}
% ============================================================

Paper 3.5$\zeta$ defines the boundary at which runtime authorization must
be verified before consequential execution.

Paper 4 begins where the question becomes:

The handoff is therefore:

\text{Authorization Enforcement Boundary}
\rightarrow

\]

The Evidence Gap remains preserved as an explicit research condition for
